This is the largest town in the Yungas region, where the high Andes descend toward the Amazon River Basin. Coroico enjoys a pleasant climate, with warm days and comfortably cool nights. There is hardly any difference between the dry season (May to December) and the rainy season (January to April). During the rainy season, rain falls almost every night, but by morning the sun breaks through the clouds and the sky turns blue. These conditions are ideal for exploring the town and its surroundings.

Coroico has plenty of hotels and restaurants serving European, Mexican and Argentine cuisine. In the evenings, visitors can enjoy the town's bars, cafés and nightclubs.

For those seeking a peaceful break, Coroico offers fresh air, warmth, wonderful views of the surrounding green mountains and a slow, sleepy, village pace of life. A leisurely stay can include trips to three waterfalls, visits to citrus and coffee plantations, or a stroll around the main square and the town's steep streets. For more active travelers, canyoning is available, with a rope descent alongside a waterfall.

### Kourou Space Centre: a visitor attraction in French Guiana

Without a long history or many historical landmarks, Kourou has become a tourist centre since the beginning of the space age.

The space centre here launches satellites and other spacecraft. Another place worth visiting is Le Vieux Bourg, a lovely spot to enjoy local food and relax.

## Cozumel: Mexico's island resort!

Cozumel is a welcoming island with around a dozen hotels and the town of San Miguel as its capital. It is Mexico's largest island, situated 19 km east of the Yucatán Peninsula, and one of the country's finest resorts. Its spectacular underwater landscapes and the world's second-largest coral reef have made it famous.

## Cozumel: an island getaway!

The island's resort life is concentrated along the west coast, where hotels and dive centres line the white sandy beaches. Cozumel is Mexico's number-one diving destination. It became a favorite international diving spot after a series of documentaries by the renowned oceanographer Jacques Cousteau. The island is home to one of Mexico's national parks, which is particularly rich in birdlife.

This place offers a glimpse of Suriname's natural side, where life is closely connected with rivers, forests and the centuries-old traditions of local communities.

Traveling to this corner of Suriname reveals a world far removed from the bustle of cities. Dense tropical vegetation, humid equatorial air and the gentle flow of the river create a sense of seclusion and harmony with nature. It is a particularly interesting place to observe the daily lives of local people, discover their customs and learn more about the country's cultural diversity.

The area around Kraka appeals to ecotourism enthusiasts and travelers keen to explore lesser-known destinations in South America. River scenery, rich greenery and abundant wildlife make a visit here an opportunity to see Suriname from an unusual perspective.

Kraka offers a chance to experience the unhurried pace of tropical life, Suriname's distinctive culture and the beauty of its unspoiled natural landscapes.

Cuenca was founded by the Spanish in 1557 on the site of an Inca city. Its historic centre retains the colonial street layout, cobbled streets, houses with balconies and inner courtyards, white churches and museums.

The Tomebamba River curves around the old part of the city and remains a distinctive feature of the urban landscape.

From Cuenca, it is easy to continue to Ingapirca, about 50 km to the north, or to the El Cajas area with its lakes and lagoons. To the northeast lie Gualaceo and Chordeleg, known for their local artists and craftspeople.
